The long IA diphthong has spelling variants including ເ◌ັຽ, ເ◌ຍ, and standalone/medial ◌ຽ in attested contexts

The spelling ເ◌ືອ represents long /ɯːə/

The implemented tone selector is scoped to Ueda's central Vientiane five-tone base system; unmarked rules distinguish live/dead syllables and vowel length, tone-marked rules apply only to live syllables, and its class/mark conditions are not a universal Lao dialect model. Ueda reports numeric contours [24], [34], [33], [21], [52]; the project converts levels 1–5 to IPA tone letters ˩ ˨ ˧ ˦ ˥, yielding ˨˦, ˧˦, ˧, ˨˩, ˥˨
The EKI/UNGEGN status report documents the BGN/PCGN 1966 Lao romanization and states that no Lao romanization system has been approved at UN conferences and Laos has no national system
The BGN/PCGN Lao romanization distinguishes syllable-initial and syllable-final consonant spellings and defines a table of vocalic nuclei
The CLDR Lao-Latin transform is marked provisional and explicitly leaves special final-consonant handling as TODO
BGN/PCGN initial spellings kh, th and ph correspond to Lao aspirated consonant letters ຂ/ຄ, ຖ/ທ and ຜ/ພ; h in these digraphs is not an independent /h/ segment
Lao /h/ onsets are represented by ຫ and ຮ, while the phonological inventory distinguishes /h/ from aspirated /kʰ/, /tʰ/ and /pʰ/
The romanization adapter validates onset spellings against the original Lao consonant grapheme and maps aspirated stops with an apostrophe while mapping independent /h/ to Ukrainian г
The CLDR/BGN romanization spelling x corresponds to Lao ຊ, whose Lao consonant value is /s/; it is not the Latin sequence /ks/
The described Lao syllable-coda inventory does not include /h/; a final h is not accepted as a supported Lao coda

The descriptive Lao orthography reference identifies restricted labialized onsets as the productive audible initial-cluster pattern and distinguishes high-class written sequences from independent /h/ clusters
The Lao letter ຣ has a modern /l/ reading in ordinary Lao, while /r/ is associated with restricted loanword or foreign-language contexts; the adapter uses /l/ as its default
The romanization adapter validates supported Lao coda graphemes against CLDR output aliases before applying position-sensitive Ukrainian coda mappings; unsupported source codas are withheld
BGN/PCGN note 5 says silent ຫ is generally omitted before the listed sonorants and that ໜ/ໝ are abbreviated forms of ຫນ/ຫມ; these are tone-class spellings, not audible h+sonorant clusters

The romanized vowel nucleus is checked against the source Lao vowel-structure ID; vowel length distinctions that the romanization collapses are not reconstructed, and unsupported or lost nuclei are withheld

The source vowel and coda distinguish Lao ກາມ (AA plus final ມ) from ກຳ (AM nucleus) even though both produce the same CLDR string kam; the source-aware parser uses those structures to resolve the romanization
In modern Ukrainian, щ represents the ordered sequence /ʃ/ plus /t͡ʃ/; the target adapter maps that exact sequence to щ while preserving standalone /ʃ/ → ш and /t͡ʃ/ → ч

In the Vientiane-oriented rule table, the rarely used modern Lao marks mai ti (໊) and mai catawa (໋) are restricted to middle-class consonants and correspond to high-falling and low-rising tones, respectively; their contours use the same Ueda numeric-to-IPA mapping [52] → ˥˨ and [24] → ˨˦
Open diphthong rhymes may form live syllables even when the nucleus has no monophthongal long-vowel mark; the Lao AM rhyme is live because it contains a nasal coda

Modern Lao tone marks are stored after the onset base consonant or a superscript vowel sign; in written onset sequences they attach to the second character, and in the AM spelling they precede the spacing AM letter
Modern Lao has a restricted set of syllable-initial labialized consonants written with a base onset followed by ວ; the listed labialized onsets do not occur before rounded vowels

BYU MATRIX Lab's Lao tonal and non-tonal IPA models use separate character-level BERT encoder-decoder sequence-to-sequence configurations; the tonal model card specifies six encoder and six decoder layers, 512 hidden size, eight attention heads and 1,024 feed-forward size. This is architecture evidence, not a linguistic rule or IPA gold.

An initial unmarked short open /a/ syllable with a core onset excluding known palatal and velar nasal C0 onsets followed by a supported major-weighted syllable is only a potential minor-syllable candidate; the engine flags it as analysis-dependent and never assigns a neutral tone
The IPA chart uses tie-bar notation to represent affricates as single segments; the project adopts t͡ɕ as canonical output for Lao ຈ while retaining untied tɕ as an accepted correspondence alias
The Unicode Lao block contains modern Lao graphemes and additional Pali Sanskrit Khmu numeric and orthographic characters; block membership is not equivalent to the modern Lao phonological inventory

An opt-in deterministic IPA profile applies high-frequency aggregate segmental correspondences observed in the pinned MekongPhon training split; it is a reference-compatibility experiment, not a universal Lao phonology claim
Lao native digits are part of the script and are commonly used
Native Lao digits are preserved unchanged as non-phonetic passthrough and are not assigned IPA
The preposed spelling ເ◌ີຍ represents the long /ɤːj/ rhyme
The preposed spelling ໂ◌ຍ represents the long /oːj/ rhyme
The preposed spelling ແ◌ວ represents the long /ɛːw/ rhyme
The postposed spelling ◌ອຍ represents the long /ɔːj/ rhyme
The postposed spelling ◌າຽ represents the long /aːj/ rhyme

Many-to-many graphoneme alignment has been evaluated on a Lao G2P dictionary and reported 91.28% word accuracy in the source paper; the reported result is not directly comparable to project benchmarks without its original split and transcription contract
SIGMORPHON 2022 provides a three-condition low-resource G2P protocol that can be adapted for Lao only as a clearly labelled non-official experiment; Lao is not an official task language
The inspected CharsiuG2P revision contains Lao WikiPron source metadata but no Lao train, development or test split; it is not a trained/evaluated Lao G2P baseline on that revision
Osatananda's analysis of one Vientiane variety treats each syllable as having an underlying lexical tone rather than deriving every tone mechanically from consonant class, rhyme and tone marks

Enfield's phonological template includes an optional minor C0V0 syllable with no independent distinctive tone; in his described variety V0 is limited to short /a i u/ and C0 to a restricted onset subset

Published Lao syllabification work and LaoNLP provide deterministic orthographic syllable segmentation examples for line-breaking/orthographic boundaries only; they do not establish lexical word segmentation, phonological source-role overlap for LOC Note 10, or IPA accuracy
Wiktextract's pronunciation fields can include output generated by Wiktionary Lua modules and therefore must not be treated uniformly as independently authored IPA gold

The pinned LaoNLP CSV has a separate MIT notice and a five-field schema, but Pronunciation is Latin romanization rather than IPA; its 21 exact repeated header rows, 3 malformed header-like rows, 3 ID-only rows, phrase entries, duplicate spellings and inconsistent Type values prevent treating it as clean word-boundary gold

Lao orthography has largely direct grapheme–phoneme correspondences, but the mapping and tone system remain dialect-sensitive; this supports an explicit dialect profile rather than one universal output

The written dialect profile reports that ໃ and ໄ are pronounced the same in Vientiane but differently in Luang Prabang; the Vientiane profile may share their phonemic output while preserving spelling provenance

Enfield's account groups Lao syllables into feet with one stressed tone-bearing syllable and potentially dependent unstressed syllables; grammatical-word boundaries do not always align with phonological-word boundaries

The historical development of Lao ຣ includes /r/ > /h/ in some conditions and /l/ elsewhere, with cluster loss and loanword complications; do not treat one unconditional /l/ rule as universally sufficient
Pali and Sanskrit loanwords form a distinct historical/orthographic layer whose pronunciation should not be inferred solely from etymological spelling using the modern native-Lao rule profile

Published Vientiane research reports carryover and anticipatory contextual effects across bitonal sequences; word-level lexical tone output should not be presented as a complete phrase-level phonetic contour

WikiPron is a Wiktionary-derived multilingual pronunciation resource, but Lao-specific coverage and provenance are not established by the inspected record; do not count it as a Lao gold or baseline yet

The BSD Lao-Dictionary word list is intended for word wrapping and mostly reduces compounds to parts; it can supply orthographic lexical hints but is not a complete lexical boundary gold set or IPA resource

A deterministic sample of 100 unique IPA-bearing Kaikki Lao forms was matched to exact Wiktionary source revisions; all 100 Lao language sections invoke lo-pron. This establishes generated template invocation in the sample, not corpus-wide per-sound provenance or exclusive source attribution because Kaikki post-processing may merge additional sources

A deterministic sample of 100 unique IPA-bearing word forms from the Kaikki Lao extraction was matched to 100 exact Wiktionary source-page revisions dated on or before the 2026-10-01 dump date; all 100 Lao language sections explicitly invoke lo-pron. Exact titles, page/revision IDs, timestamps and source-text lengths match the manifest 100/100. This establishes template invocation in the sample, but not corpus-wide provenance or exclusive attribution of every Kaikki sound value because Kaikki post-processing may merge additional sources.

LaoNLP is not a drop-in implementation of ALA-LC Note 9: its word tokenizer uses maximum-match over a composite dictionary rather than the LOC shortest-standalone-written-form and loanword-specific rules; its regex syllable tokenizer is for orthographic line breaking, not phonological double-function roles
ALA-LC 2012 Note 8 maps Lao digits ໐–໙ to Arabic numerals 0–9 in Lao-source romanization

HVULao_NLP publishes human-reviewed Lao word-segmentation guidelines based on minimal orthographic units carrying lexical or grammatical meaning, context-sensitive decisions and explicit compound/function-word handling; this is a comparative candidate for LOC Note 9, not a demonstrated implementation of the LOC loanword clauses

A Lao language-specific orthography reference distinguishes Pali/Sanskrit borrowings from more recent foreign loans in the use of ລ versus ຣ, while a manuscript-cataloguing convention records both historically conservative Indic spellings and modernized forms for lexicalized common loans; origin and lexicalization therefore require lexeme-level evidence and cannot be inferred mechanically from one grapheme

The pinned ICU Lao dictionary is a word-break resource created for word wrapping; it may be evaluated as a lexical hint but must not be treated as ALA-LC Note 9 gold or a complete Pali/Sanskrit and other-loanword boundary policy

On 839 of 1,000 HVULao_NLP test sentence pairs whose raw and segmented forms concatenate identically after NFC and whitespace removal, greedy longest-prefix matching over 30,550 unique ICU Lao dictionary entries achieved micro boundary precision 0.8353, recall 0.8940 and F1 0.8636; greedy shortest-prefix matching achieved precision 0.3450, recall 0.9985 and F1 0.5129. Scores cover 49,608 adjacent Lao-character boundary positions only and are not comparable to the paper's 0.75 model F1. Neither strategy implements LOC Note 9.

The LOC 2012 Note 10 gives the romanized example khitsatān and specifies repeated romanization when one consonant serves as the coda of one syllable and onset of the next. The exact Lao glyph sequence is unresolved: the currently retrievable PDF text extraction and rendered page do not yet support a single confidently verified transcription, and LOC identifies the unavailable Word source as preferred. This does not establish the project's automatic source-script syllabification or role analysis

The Informatica article is published under CC BY 3.0 while the separate Mendeley Data v2 corpus record lists CC BY 4.0; the paper states underlying source websites permitted research and non-commercial text reuse, so neither publication licence alone establishes commercial redistribution rights for the underlying source texts

The Library of Congress currently lists the 2012 Lao Romanization Table as the current table and 1997 only as an earlier reference version; LOC says earlier versions are for reference only and not for current cataloging

The Library of Congress identifies Microsoft Word source documents as the files from which ALA-LC tables are created and instructs users to copy from those source documents rather than PDF versions; the Lao source DOC link was not retrievable in this audit and remains uninspected

The current UNGEGN index places Lao v4.0 (2013) under other languages/scripts, not among the systems recommended by the United Nations; the 2025 WGRS report says that as of July 2024 Lao PDR was finalizing draft toponymy guidelines and that consideration at the 2027 UNGEGN Session was hoped for. The 2023 WGRS minutes describe ministry feedback and a draft awaiting government approval; the 2025 country-name record still uses BGN/PCGN 1966 for the country's formal name. These sources establish ongoing development and continued use of a legacy toponymic convention, not a finalized or adopted universal Lao transcription standard or a Ukrainian target standard.

For the described central Vientiane Lao variety, written consonant-letter sequences do not establish spoken consonant clusters: Ueda reports no phonological consonant clusters and shows written w corresponding to /ua/ or no independent spoken segment in cited forms. This is dialect-scoped phonological evidence, not a complete orthographic syllabification algorithm

Berment (2004) documents a historical explicit grammar for Lao orthographic syllable candidates, with onset/consonant groups, positional vowel patterns, optional accent and restricted coda; the thesis reports theoretical unattested outputs and simplified accent placement, so it is a research basis rather than a current validated Lao spelling standard

Berment (2004) models candidate syllables as edges in a text-position graph, removes candidates that cannot participate in a complete path, and preserves ambiguous regions; its longest-candidate choice is a local UI selection heuristic, not an established global linguistic resolver

The historical Berment grammar reportedly generates 56,670 candidate Lao syllable strings and a 33-state/480-transition minimal automaton, but accepts theoretical unattested forms and simplifies accent constraints; historical figures are not current repository benchmarks or proof of contemporary orthographic coverage

Del Vigna and Berment (2003) formalize a finite language of irreducible ambiguous strings for a historical Lao syllable dictionary; the reported dictionary and automaton counts describe that study only and do not resolve lexical or phonological interpretation for current input

The ICANN Lao root-zone rules encode a limited ordering framework: U+0EBC follows a consonant; vowel-before precedes the main consonant cluster; above/below vowels follow the main consonant; vowel-after follows the main consonant, tone mark or vowel-above; tone marks follow the main consonant or above/below vowels; cancellation mark follows a final consonant; repetition mark is constrained at label end

ICANN explicitly leaves many Lao spelling constraints unenforced in the Root Zone LGR, including regular-syllable consonant combinations because arbitrary sequences occur in acronyms; vowel/diphthong combinations are also over-produced to limit WLE complexity. The LGR must not be treated as a complete syllable recognizer or spelling validator

The 2026 W3C Lao layout-requirements Group Note Draft describes Lao as an alphabet with explicit vowels, no conjuncts except the HA subjoined consonant case, pre-base vowel glyphs, spacing and combining vowel components, and multipart vowels that can surround base consonants; this is technical layout guidance, not an endorsed linguistic spelling standard

The 2025 ICANN RZ-LGR-6 Lao ruleset is scoped to DNS root-zone labels and Unicode 16.0; its 51-code-point repertoire, one sequence and nine rules are implementation constraints for that domain, not an exhaustive inventory or validation policy for arbitrary Lao text

Ishida (2026) describes modern Lao as an alphabet with explicit vowels and a restricted coda inventory, making individual syllable boundaries comparatively straightforward to identify; multi-syllabic lexical word boundaries still require a dictionary or explicit ZWSP and must not be conflated with syllable segmentation

Ishida (2026) distinguishes audible onset labialization formed by an onset consonant followed by ວ from written high-class ຫ-plus-consonant sequences (including ຫຼ with U+0EBC); these must be kept as onset units, without generalizing beyond the listed labialized-onset inventory

A Lao pre-base vowel is stored before the entire syllable onset, including a multi-character onset; tone marks and post-base vowel signs attach to the second/phonological consonant in such an onset, as illustrated by ໃຫຍ່ and ເຫຼືອງ

Unicode grapheme clusters do not correspond one-to-one with Lao orthographic syllables: pre-base vowel letters and post-base spacing components may be separate text units, while combining marks attach to a base; syllable onset clusters also have distinct grouping rules

Ishida (2026) lists nine consonant graphemes in modern Lao syllable-final position (ບ ດ ກ ມ ນ ຣ ງ ວ ຍ), notes that coda sounds may differ from onset values, and identifies U+0EB3 as a special -am rhyme representation; this orthographic coda spelling inventory is distinct from the project's IPA-final mapping and the broader ICANN root-zone label repertoire
